name: Tasmanian, language
confidence_why: No source describes stress in the north-western language itself: Crowley and Dixon (1981) call stress the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology and conclude only that any syllable but the last can bear it, working mainly from eastern and south-eastern records, while Taylor (2006) reads the same nineteenth-century wordlist marks as regular initial stress and Ritz (1909) as frequent antepenultimate or speaker-variable accent, so any placement for Northwestern Tasmanian would be a guess.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. Tasmanian. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Volume 2, 394-421 (references 422-427). Canberra: Australian National University Press. Open scan: ANU Open Research hdl:1885/114846 (copy consulted).
catalog_locator: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (the whole section sits on this page, 2.5 Phonotactics opens p. 414); scope statement section 2.1 p. 407; language inventory section 1.4 p. 403 (language (f)); west-coast consonant-final remark section 2.5 p. 414.
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.1 of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positive rule. Working from 19th-century recorders' accent diacritics (Walker, Norman), Milligan's orthographic remark, Tindale's transcriptions, the Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and Crowley's 1972 recordings of two descendants, the authors infer that disyllables are initially stressed and trisyllables are stressed on the first or the second syllable with no conditioning given; the only general conclusion is negative: stress never falls on the final syllable. Stated for the Tasmanian languages collectively, with the phonology 'based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages' (p. 407); none of the six evidence sources is north-western.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Crowley & Dixon. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis, pp. 160, 257-259) reads the same diacritics as strong stress on the first word element with at best secondary stress on later elements, pan-Palawa; Ritz 1909 pp. 48-49 claims frequent antepenultimate accent and free placement. Neither is north-western-specific.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the disyllable/trisyllable observations are hedged ('it appears') and the authors decline to state a rule. Related remark p. 414: consonant-final words 'come almost exclusively from the dialects of the west coast', possibly with a weakly articulated underlying final vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word ('The position of stress within a word'); reconstructed from written wordlist citation forms and a handful of 20th-century recordings, no living speakers. Areal statement for 'Tasmanian' as a whole applied to a languoid the chapter subsumes as language (f) 'North-western, Robbins Island, Circular Head' (p. 403).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nort3415 = ISO 639-3 xpw 'Northwestern Tasmanian / Peerapper' (AIATSIS T3, T6, T11, T12), created by ISO CR 2019-047 from Bowern 2012's Western cluster ('the northwestern and southwestern tribes'; sister of sout3391 Southwestern Tasmanian). In Crowley & Dixon 1981 it corresponds to language (f) 'North-western, Robbins Island, Circular Head' (p. 403), known from Robinson's 1829-34 lists, Jorgenson's Circular Head list, and possibly Milligan's Flinders-Island 'north-west and western tribes' list, which C&D say 'does not correspond too well with earlier vocabularies from these areas' (p. 397) and which Bowern assigns to her northern cluster instead. The quoted stress statement is for 'Tasmanian' collectively, drawn from eastern and Bass Strait evidence, and is the identical passage already recorded for the sibling keys sout1439, sout3391, neta1235, brun1235 and the bookkeeping key tasm1247; it is not a description of the north-western language.

tone_statements.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania (UTAS figshare doi:10.25959/23206187.v1).
tone_statements.quote: There can be little doubt that tone played a semantic role in the Palawa languages. Examples are provided in Part A of Table 7. 1 1 . But there is no evidence ofthe use oftone as a systematic contrasting semantic device, as in the Sino-Tibetan languages. It is therefore inferred that the Palawa use of tone differed little from its use in English. In other words, tone would have indicated a speaker' s mood, but was rarely capable of transcription by the European recorder.

sources.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania (UTAS figshare doi:10.25959/23206187.v1).
sources.note: Section 7.9 Stress and Accenting pp. 257-259: rejects Crowley & Dixon ('I am unable to agree with any of these observations'); from the recorders' bar/breve diacritics 'in 99 per cent of word elements in initial position.. the first vowel is marked with a bar', 'completely consistent with strong stressing of the first word element in words'; Dixon's mainland alternating cadence does not apply. Pan-Palawa reanalysis of the same written records; no north-western data; non-linguist MA thesis.

tone.says: Section 7.11 'Tone': from the 19th-century records there is no evidence that tone was used as a systematic contrastive device; Taylor infers that tone functioned as in English (affect/intonation), untranscribable by the recorders, and turns to onomatopoeia. I.e. an explicit 'no lexical tone (as far as the record shows)' statement for the Tasmanian languages as a group.

sources.citation: Ritz, Hermann B. 1909. The speech of the Tasmanian Aborigines. Papers & Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania for 1908: 44-81.
sources.note: pp. 48-49: recorders mark accent by doubling the following consonant or a stroke over the vowel; 'the Tasmanian word-accent was quite frequently on the third syllable from the end, the antepenult'; suggests speakers were 'free to accentuate a word at random or at will'. Antiquarian, pan-Tasmanian, no north-western data.
